l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythian games crown victors with wreath of beech leaves (for feats of strength, running, or chariot racing)
q: In commemoration of this illustrious conquest he instituted the Pythian games, in which the victor in feats of strength, swiftness of foot, or in the chariot race, was crowned with a wreath of beech leaves; for the laurel was not yet adopted by Apollo as his own tree.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Apollo founds Delphic oracle (at Delphi)
q: And here Apollo founded his oracle at Delphi, the only oracle "that was not exclusively national, for it was consulted by many outside nations, and, in fact, was held in the highest repute all over the world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Delphic oracle is consulted by many outside nations (as a widely respected oracle)
q: And here Apollo founded his oracle at Delphi, the only oracle "that was not exclusively national, for it was consulted by many outside nations, and, in fact, was held in the highest repute all over the world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Delphic oracle guides Greek colonies (its decrees were followed in founding the earliest colonies)
q: In obedience to its decrees, the laws of Lycurgus were introduced, and the earliest Greek colonies founded.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Delphi contains Delphic oracle
q: And here Apollo founded his oracle at Delphi, the only oracle "that was not exclusively national, for it was consulted by many outside nations, and, in fact, was held in the highest repute all over the world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Greek sculpture uses bronze casting (one of three important processes)
q: From the sixth century before Christ date three processes of great importance in the development of sculpture; the art of casting in bronze, the chiselling of marble, and the inlaying of gold and ivory on wood (chryselephantine work).

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ageladas is a sculptor (at Argus)
q: At Argus, contemporary with these early schools of Athens and Aegina, was a school of artists depending on the fame of the great sculptor Ageladas.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ageladas teaches Myron
q: his great distinction is not through works of his own, but is due to the fact that he was the teacher of Myron, Polycleitos, and Pheidias.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ageladas teaches Polycleitos
q: his great distinction is not through works of his own, but is due to the fact that he was the teacher of Myron, Polycleitos, and Pheidias.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ageladas teaches Pheidias
q: his great distinction is not through works of his own, but is due to the fact that he was the teacher of Myron, Polycleitos, and Pheidias.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Myron surpasses Pythagoras (in vivid naturalness)
q: In this vivid naturalness Pythagoras was himself far surpassed by Myron.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Discobolos is copied at Vatican (one copy)
q: one being at the Vatican, the other at the Palazzo Massimi alle Colonne.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Greek sculpture uses marble sculpture (one of three important processes)
q: From the sixth century before Christ date three processes of great importance in the development of sculpture; the art of casting in bronze, the chiselling of marble, and the inlaying of gold and ivory on wood (chryselephantine work).

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Discobolos is copied at Palazzo Massimi alle Colonne (one copy)
q: one being at the Vatican, the other at the Palazzo Massimi alle Colonne.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Polycleitos creates Doryphoros (model of the human figure)
q: Perfection of form was his aim, and so nearly did he seem to the ancients to have attained this object that his Doryphoros was taken by them as a model of the human figure.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Doryphoros is a statue of a youth bearing a lance (quiet and reserved pose)
q: A copy of this statue exists in the Museum of Naples and represents a youth in the attitude of bearing a lance, quiet and reserved.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pheidias is a Athenian (by birth)
q: Pheidias was an Athenian by birth, the son of Charmides.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pheidias directs his great monumental works (at Athens)
q: when Pericles wanted a director for his great monumental works at Athens, he summoned Pheidias.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pheidias creates Minerva of the Parthenon (highest conception of divinity)
q: It was reserved for Pheidias to portray the highest conceptions of divinity of which the Greek mind was capable in his statues of Athene in the Parthenon at Athens, and the Zeus of Olympus

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pheidias creates Parthenon frieze (under his supervision)
q: The frieze of the Parthenon, executed under the supervision of Pheidias, represented one of the most glorious religious ceremonies of the Greek, the Pan-Athenaic procession.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Greek sculpture uses chryselephantine sculpture (one of three important processes)
q: From the sixth century before Christ date three processes of great importance in the development of sculpture; the art of casting in bronze, the chiselling of marble, and the inlaying of gold and ivory on wood (chryselephantine work).

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pericles turns to the artistic development of the city (after Athens's leadership was established)
q: when th leadership of Athens in Greece had become firmly established under Theistocles and Cimon, the third president of the democracy, Pericles, found leisure to turn to the artistic development of the city.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pericles becomes president of Athens (in 444 B.C.)
q: Pericles became president of the city in 444 B.C., just at the time when the decorative arts were approaching perfection under Pheidias.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Parthenon is honored to Athene (guardian deity of Athens)
q: The Parthenon was fashioned in honor of Athene or Minerva, the guardian deity of Athens, the preserver of Hellas

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Parthenon contains Pan-Athenaic procession (represented on its frieze)
q: The frieze of the Parthenon, executed under the supervision of Pheidias, represented one of the most glorious religious ceremonies of the Greek, the Pan-Athenaic procession.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pan-Athenaic procession is represented on Parthenon frieze
q: The frieze of the Parthenon, executed under the supervision of Pheidias, represented one of the most glorious religious ceremonies of the Greek, the Pan-Athenaic procession.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Parthenon frieze depicts Pan-Athenaic procession (including virgins, animals, musicians, chariots, and riders)
q: The deities surround Zeus as spectators of the scene, and toward them winds the long line of virgins bearing incense, herds of animals for sacrifice, players upon the lute and lyre, chariots and riders.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: British Museum contains Parthenon frieze (larger part preserved there)
q: The larger part of this frieze has been preserved and is to be seen at the British Museum.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: British Museum contains Parthenon pediments (fragments purchased by Lord Elgin)
q: The fragments were purchased by Lord Elgin early in this century and are now in the British Museum.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Greek sculpture is a natural art (even in primitive forms)
q: Greek sculpture, on the contrary, even in its primitive forms was eminently natural, capable of developing a high degree of realism.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: bronze casting originates in Samos (probably)
q: To the Samians is probably due the invention of bronze casting, to the Chians the beginning of sculpture in marble.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: marble sculpture originates in Chios (probably)
q: To the Samians is probably due the invention of bronze casting, to the Chians the beginning of sculpture in marble.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: chryselephantine sculpture originates in Crete
q: Chryselephantine sculpture began in Crete.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: British Museum contains Payne-Knight Apollo (among ancient monuments suggestive of Canachos’s style)
q: among which are the Payne-Knight Apollo at the British Museum, and the Piombino Apollo at the Louvre.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pheidias has fame based on Athene Promachos (among three great works)
q: The fame of Pheidias himself, however, rested very largely on three great pieces of art work: The Athene Promachos, the Athene Parthenos, and the Olympian Zeus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Athene Promachos has surviving copy no copy (no copy survives)
q: No copy of this statue survives, and hence a description of it must be largely conjectural, made up from hints gleaned from Athenian coins.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Athene Promachos is described from Athenian coins (largely conjecturally)
q: No copy of this statue survives, and hence a description of it must be largely conjectural, made up from hints gleaned from Athenian coins.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Minerva of the Parthenon is a statue
q: Pheidias sculptured other statues of Athene, but none so wonderful as the Athene Parthenos, which, with the Olympian Zeus, was the wonder and admiration of the Greek world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Minerva of the Parthenon is wonder of Greek world (together with the Olympian Zeus)
q: Pheidias sculptured other statues of Athene, but none so wonderful as the Athene Parthenos, which, with the Olympian Zeus, was the wonder and admiration of the Greek world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Minerva of the Parthenon symbolizes Athene (as an outward symbol of her divinity)
q: The Athene Parthenos was designed to stand as an outward symbol of the divinity in whose protecting might the city had conquered and grown strong, in whose honor the temple had been built in which this statue was to shine as queen.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Minerva of the Parthenon is chryselephantine chryselephantine sculpture
q: Both the Olympian Zeus and the Athene were of chryselephantine work offering enormous technical difficulties, but in spite of this both showed almost absolute perfection of form united with beauty of intellectual character to represent the godhead incarnate in human substance.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter represents that greater divinity (honored by all Hellas)
q: The Olympian Zeus was the representative of that greater divinity which all Hellas united in honoring.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter is representative of Jupiter (the greater divinity honored throughout Hellas)
q: The Olympian Zeus was the representative of that greater divinity which all Hellas united in honoring.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter is wonder of Greek world (together with the Athene Parthenos)
q: Pheidias sculptured other statues of Athene, but none so wonderful as the Athene Parthenos, which, with the Olympian Zeus, was the wonder and admiration of the Greek world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter has material ivory and gold (including its throne)
q: Zeus," says Pausanias, "is seated on a throne of ivory and gold; upon his head is laced a garland made in imitation of olive leaves

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pheidias has fame based on Minerva of the Parthenon (among three great works)
q: The fame of Pheidias himself, however, rested very largely on three great pieces of art work: The Athene Promachos, the Athene Parthenos, and the Olympian Zeus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter has attribute Victory (held in the right hand, crowned and made in gold and ivory)
q: He bears a Victory in his right hand, also crowned and made in gold and ivory, and holding in her right hand a little fillet.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter has attribute sceptre (held in the left hand and made of all kinds of metals)
q: In his left hand the god holds a sceptre, made of all kinds of metals; the bird perched on the tip of the sceptre is an eagle.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter has attribute eagle (perched on the tip of the sceptre)
q: In his left hand the god holds a sceptre, made of all kinds of metals; the bird perched on the tip of the sceptre is an eagle.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter has material gold (shoes, mantle, and inlaid decorations)
q: The shoes of Zeus are also of gold, and of gold his mantle, and underneath this mantle are figures and lilies inlaid.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter is chryselephantine chryselephantine sculpture
q: Both the Olympian Zeus and the Athene were of chryselephantine work offering enormous technical difficulties, but in spite of this both showed almost absolute perfection of form united with beauty of intellectual character to represent the godhead incarnate in human substance.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter has form almost absolute perfection (united with beauty of intellectual character)
q: Both the Olympian Zeus and the Athene were of chryselephantine work offering enormous technical difficulties, but in spite of this both showed almost absolute perfection of form united with beauty of intellectual character to represent the godhead incarnate in human substance.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Olympian Jupiter adds to religion (through its beauty, according to Quintilian)
q: The beauty of the Olympian Zeus, according to Quintilian, "added a new element to religion."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pheidias has fame based on Olympian Jupiter (among three great works)
q: The fame of Pheidias himself, however, rested very largely on three great pieces of art work: The Athene Promachos, the Athene Parthenos, and the Olympian Zeus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Apollo has pose calm and commanding (in the western pediment)
q: In the latter the action is extremely violent, only the Apollo in the midst is calm and commanding.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Athene Promachos represents Athene (standing and gazing toward Athens)
q: It represented the goddess standing gazing toward Athens lovingly and protectingly.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Athene Promachos has height nine feet
q: The statue was nine feet high.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Athene Promachos has style dignified and noble
q: It was dignified and noble, but at the time of its conception Pheidias had not freed himself from the convention and traditions of the earlier school, and the stiff folds of the tunic, the cold demeanor of the goddess, recall the masters whom Pheidias was destined to supersede.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Athene Promachos has attribute spear (held in one hand)
q: She held a spear in one hand, the other supported a buckler.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Athene Promachos has attribute buckler (supported by the other hand)
q: She held a spear in one hand, the other supported a buckler.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Greek sculpture declines after Peloponnesian war (with seeds of decay ripening rapidly)
q: But from the time of the Peloponnesian war, the seeds of decay were in the art of Hellas, and they ripened fast.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: sculpture expresses permanent character (rather than temporary accidental feeling)
q: Sculpture is fitted to express not temporary, accidental feeling, but permanent character; not violent action, but repose.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: sculpture expresses repose (rather than violent action)
q: Sculpture is fitted to express not temporary, accidental feeling, but permanent character; not violent action, but repose.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: later Greek school lacks repose and entire assurance (in comparison with earlier sculpture)
q: The later sculpture, therefore, lacks in some measure the repose and entire assurance of the earlier.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: later Greek school elaborates details and elements of stories and characters (in its subjects)
q: The latter dealt in great elaboration with the details and elements of the stories and characters that formed its subjects, as in the Niobe group, or the Laocoon, to be mentioned later.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Kephisodotos is a Athenian sculptor (possibly the father of Praxiteles)
q: Between these, however, and the earlier school which they superseded came the Athenian Kephisodotos, the father, it may be supposed of Praxiteles.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Kephisodotos creates Eirene and Ploutos (his single famous work)
q: His fame rests upon a single work, a copy of which has been discovered, the Eirene and Ploutos.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Scopas is a Greek sculptor (born at Paros and active in the first half of the fourth century)
q: Scopas was born at Paros, and lived during the fist half of the fourth century.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Scopas decorates temple of Athena at Tegea (including its pediments)
q: He did much decorative work including the pediments of the temple of Athena at Tegea.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Scopas participates in Mausoleum (its decoration)
q: He participated also in the decoration of the Mausoleum erected by Artemisia to the memory of her husband.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Scopas is attributed creator of Niobe group (the group is attributed to him)
q: The fame of Scopas rests principally on the Niobe group which is attributed to him.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Niobe group depicts Niobe (during the slaughter of her children)
q: The sculpture represents the wife of Amphion at the moment when the curse of Apollo and Diana falls upon her, and her children are slain before her eyes.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Niobe group is a grandly tragic sculpture (free from contortion)
q: The whole group is free from contortion and grandly tragic.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Niobe group survives as copies of parts (in the Uffizi Gallery at Florence)
q: The original exists no longer, but copies of parts of the group are found in the Uffizi Gallery at Florence.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Praxiteles is a Greek sculptor (of the later Greek type)
q: These modern tendencies produced as the greatest artists of the later Greek type Scopas and Praxiteles.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Praxiteles has work one statue (from the master's own hand)
q: Of the work of Praxiteles we know more directly than of the work of any other Greek sculptor of the same remoteness, for one statue has come down to us actually from the master's own hand, and we possess good copies of several others.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Praxiteles creates Aphrodite of Cnidos (one of at least five Aphrodites)
q: His statues of Aphrodite, of which there were at least five, are known to us by the figures on coins and by two works in the same style, the Aphrodite in the Glyptothek, and that of the Vatican. The most famous of all was the Aphrodite of Cnidos, which was ranked with the Olympian Zeus and was called one of the wonders of te world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Aphrodite of Cnidos is a wonder of the world (ranked with the Olympian Zeus)
q: The most famous of all was the Aphrodite of Cnidos, which was ranked with the Olympian Zeus and was called one of the wonders of te world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Praxiteles creates Apollo with the Lizard (a graceful masculine figure)
q: Another of his masculine figures is the graceful Apollo with the Lizard.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Praxiteles creates Satyr (transforming the satyr into a graceful youth)
q: The Satyr, in the hands of Praxiteles, lost all his ancient uncouthness, and became a strong, graceful youth, with soft, full form.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Hermes of Olympia illustrates sensual loveliness (of the later school)
q: Nevertheless, the Hermes illustrates sensual loveliness of the later school.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Hermes of Olympia supports Bacchus (as a protector)
q: He stands leaning easily against a tree, supporting on one arm the child Dionysus, to whom he turns his gracious head with the devotion and love of a protector.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Hermes of Olympia depicts beautiful man (without traditional divine symbols)
q: The god is without the traditional symbols of his divinity. He is merely a beautiful man.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Victory of Samothrace is a work of an unknown artist (probably a follower of Scopas)
q: Another work of an unknown artist, probably a follower of Scopas, is the splendid Victory of Samothrace, now in the Louvre.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Venus of Melos is a statue (of doubtful proper title and attribution)
q: Another statue which belongs, so far as artistic reasoning may carry us, to the period and school of Praxiteles, is the so- called Venus of Milo.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Venus of Melos represents ideal of purity and sweetness (with maidenly dignity)
q: It represents an ideal of purity and sweetness.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Lysippos of Sikyou is a last great sculptor of Greece
q: The last of the great sculptors of Greece was Lysippos of Sikyou.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Lysippos of Sikyou differs from Pheidias (by representing gods as exaggerated human beings)
q: Pheidias strove to make his gods all god-like; Lysippos was content to represent them merely as exaggerated human beings

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Lysippos of Sikyou sets standard human perfection (higher than average human examples)
q: Lysippos felt that he must set the standard of human perfection higher than it appears in the average of human examples.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Lysippos of Sikyou creates Hercules (with superhuman manly strength)
q: Hence we have from him the statues of Heracles, in which the ideal of manly strength was carried far beyond the range of human possibility.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Dying Gladiator represents Wounded Gaul (a Gaul sinking wounded to the ground)
q: One of the most famous works which they have left is the figure long known as the Dying Gladiator, of which a copy exists in the Capitoline Museum. This represents a Gaul sinking wounded to the ground, supporting himself on his right arm.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Dying Gladiator is marked by stern realism
q: It is remarkable for its stern realism.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Laocoon is produced in Rhodes (one of two famous sculpture groups)
q: Two of the most famous sculpture groups in the world were produced at Rhodes, the Laocoon, now at the Vatican, and the Farnese Bull, now at Naples.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Laocoon is created by Agesandros (with Athanodorus and Polydorus)
q: The former was the work of three artists, given by Pliny as Agesandros, Athanodorus, and Polydorus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Laocoon exemplifies pathetic tendency in sculpture (at its utmost)
q: The Laocoon illustrates excellently the extreme results of the pathetic tendency.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Laocoon is a tour de force (with little serious meaning)
q: In this way the work became a superb piece of display, a TOUR DE FORCE of surprising composition but with little serious meaning.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Farnese Bull is created by Apollonius (with Tauriscos of Tralles)
q: The same judgment may be extended to the Farnese Bull, the work of Apollonius and Tauriscos, artists from Tralles who lived at Rhodes.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Farnese Bull represents punishment of Dirke (at the hands of the sons of Antiope)
q: This group represents the punishment of the cruel Dirke at the hands of the sons of Antiope.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Farnese Bull is a failure failure (judged on general lines despite marvellous technical skill)
q: Altogether, the group, in spite of the marvellous technical skill shown in details, is a failure when judged on general lines.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Venus de' Medici is a degenerate and sensuous conception (of the final period of Greek art)
q: To the same period also belongs almost the last notable work of Greek art, the degenerate and sensuous conception of the Venus de Medici.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Rome becomes chief seat of Greek sculpture production (after Greek artists began moving there)
q: in time Greek artists also began to remove thither, so that Rome became not only the centre for the collection of Greek works of art, but the chief seat of their production.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Greek sculpture declines into dilettantism and weakness (under Roman influence)
q: The influence of the Greeks upon Rome was very marked, but the reflex influence of the material civilization of Italy upon Greek art was altogether bad, and thus the splendor of classical art went out in dilletantism and weakness.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Greek mythology provides subject-matter for painters and sculptors (from the Renaissance onward)
q: Then, indeed, by the discovery and circulation of the poets of mythology, the Greek stories and conceptions of characters, divine and human, became known once more and were used freely, remaining until the present day one chief source of material and subject-matter for the use of the painter and sculptor.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Agoracritos produces works indistinguishable from Pheidias (in perfection)
q: Agoracritos left behind him works at Athens which in their perfection could scarcely be distinguished from the works of Pheidias himself, none of which have come down to us.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Jupiter is husband of Juno
q: Jupiter and Juno, although husband and wife, did not live together very happily.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Juno places eyes on peacock (as ornaments on its tail)
q: Juno took them and put them as ornaments on the tail of her peacock, where they remain to this day.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Io is daughter of Inachus (a river god)
q: This was indeed the case; for it was Io, the daughter of the river god Inachus, whom Jupiter had been flirting with, and, when he became aware of the approach of his wife, had changed into that form.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Io is daughter of Inachus
q: This was indeed the case; for it was Io, the daughter of the river god Inachus, whom Jupiter had been flirting with, and, when he became aware of the approach of his wife, had changed into that form.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Io is restored to human form former self (after Juno consents)
q: At length Jupiter interceded for her, and, upon his promising not to pay her any more attentions, Juno consented to restore her to her form.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Argus is a guardian (of Io)
q: The goddess was not yet relieved of her suspicions; and she delivered the heifer to Argus, to be strictly watched.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Argus has a hundred eyes (in his head)
q: Now Argus had a hundred eyes in his head, and never went to sleep with more than two at a time

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Mercury wears winged slippers (on his feet)
q: Mercury made haste, put his winged slippers on his feet, and cap on his head, took his sleep-producing wand, and leaped down from the heavenly towers to the earth.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Syrinx is a nymph (a faithful worshipper of Diana)
q: There was a certain nymph, whose name was Syrinx, who was much beloved by the satyrs and spirits of the wood; but she would have none of them, but was a faithful worshipper of Diana, and followed the chase.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable

s: Sicily is returned to by Ceres (after passing from land to land, and across seas and rivers)
q: Ceres continued her search for her daughter, passing from land to land, and across seas and rivers, till at length she returned to Sicily

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Proserpine is released partially Ceres (spending half her time with her mother)
q: she was to pass half the time with her mother, and the rest with her husband Pluto.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Proserpine eats pomegranate (in the lower world)
q: the maiden had taken a pomegranate which Pluto offered her, and had sucked the sweet pulp from a few of the seeds.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Proserpine symbolizes seed-corn (in the allegory)
q: Proserpine signifies the seed-corn, which, when cast into the ground, lies there concealed

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pluto is a ruler of Tartarus (underworld monarch)
q: yonder dark monarch, who rules the realm of Tartarus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pluto possesses Pluto's chariot (drawn by four black horses)
q: He mounts his chariot with the four black horses and comes up to earth and looks around.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pygmalion is a sculptor
q: He was a sculptor, and had made with wonderful skill a statue of ivory, so beautiful that no living woman could be compared to it in beauty.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Venus blesses Pygmalion and Galatea's union (as goddess of the nuptials)
q: Venus blessed the nuptials she had formed, and from this union Paphos was born, from whom the city, sacred to Venus, received its name.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Schiller applies Pygmalion myth (to the love of nature in a youthful heart)
q: Schiller, in his poem, the Ideals, applies this tale of Pygmalion to the love of nature in a youthful heart.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: William Morris describes Pygmalion myth (in Earthly Paradise)
q: Morris tells the story of Pygmalion and the Image in some of the most beautiful verses of the Earthly Paradise.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Dryope is a wife (wife of Andraemon)
q: Dryope and Iole were sisters. The former was the wife of Andraemon, beloved by her husband, and happy in the birth of her first child.
